paragraphs: Adaptive importance sampling repeatedly changes where it draws samples using information collected so far. Each stage combines exploration, which generates points under the current sampling policy, with an update that uses accumulated information to improve that policy. The paper studies the behavior of empirical sums built from this changing sequence of sampling distributions.

The central theoretical result is asymptotic optimality: as sampling continues, the method has the same asymptotic behavior as an oracle strategy that knew the targeted sampling policy from the start. The analysis places no assumptions on the allocation of sample counts across stages. Consequently, its treatment does not require a prescribed division of computational resources between drawing samples and updating the policy.

The paper also introduces weighted adaptive importance sampling, which allows poor samples from early stages to be forgotten. This addresses the practical fact that early sampling policies can be less useful than later ones. Together, the contributions connect a long-run optimality result with a mechanism for reducing the influence of an initially weak sampling strategy.
neurips-2018-asymptotic-optimality-of-ad.tldr: Adaptive importance sampling can asymptotically match an oracle sampling strategy without a prescribed allocation of samples across stages.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Gaussian process approach to learning from graph data when only some nodes have labels. Its construction brings together node features and network connectivity within a Bayesian model. The aim is to make effective use of limited labels while accounting for the relationships represented by the graph.

The model has two complementary interpretations. One views it as regression on empirical distributions, with local graph connections determining how information is weighted. The other starts from a Bayesian linear model in which node features are filtered using an operator related to the graph Laplacian. These interpretations explain how graph structure enters the prediction process. Implementation can build on existing scalable variational inference methods for Gaussian processes.

On semi-supervised benchmarks, the model is highly competitive with leading graph neural networks. In active learning experiments with scarce labels, it outperforms those neural networks. It also avoids needing a separate validation dataset for early stopping to control overfitting, a useful property when labeled data are already limited.
neurips-2018-bayesian-semi-supervised-le.tldr: A graph Gaussian process combines node features and connectivity to learn efficiently from scarce labels.

paragraphs: BRUNO is a deep recurrent architecture for reasoning about sets of complex, high-dimensional observations. Its defining property is exchangeability: changing the order of observations leaves their joint probability unchanged. This matters when the observations should be treated as a set, even though a recurrent model processes them through a sequence.

The architecture supports exact Bayesian inference within its model and does not require variational approximations for training. It can also generate new observations conditioned on examples already seen. The computational cost of that conditional generation grows linearly with the number of conditioning examples, giving a stated scaling relationship as more evidence is supplied.

The paper demonstrates the architecture on conditional image generation, few-shot learning, and anomaly detection. These tasks share a need to generalize from short observed sequences while representing variability among possible observations. BRUNO's contribution is to combine that flexibility with a provable ordering invariance, so the probabilistic treatment of a collection does not depend on which example happens to be presented first.
neurips-2018-bruno-a-deep-recurrent-mode.tldr: BRUNO combines deep recurrent modeling with exact Bayesian inference and a provably order-invariant distribution over observations.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decisions in which a learner chooses a set of options each round using contextual information about those options. Two complications occur together: the available options can change, and the reward of a selected set depends on relationships among its members. In particular, overlapping or redundant choices can produce diminishing returns.

These features arise in applications such as recommendation and crowdsourcing. An option that is useful alone may add less value when similar options have already been selected, while changing availability prevents the learner from relying on a fixed menu. The proposed CC-MAB algorithm addresses context, set selection, changing availability, and submodular rewards within one stochastic bandit framework.

The paper proves a regret bound of O(c T^((2α+D)/(3α+D)) log(T)) over T rounds. This quantifies how the algorithm's cumulative decision shortfall scales within the analyzed setting. Experiments on a real crowdsourcing dataset also show better performance than prior approaches. The contribution is both an online policy for the combined problem and a theoretical analysis that treats its interacting complications together.
neurips-2018-contextual-combinatorial-mu.tldr: CC-MAB selects changing sets of contextual options while accounting for diminishing returns, with a regret guarantee and supporting crowdsourcing results.

paragraphs: The predictive coding network recognizes objects through repeated exchanges between neighboring layers. Higher layers send predictions downward, while lower layers send prediction errors upward. These local feedback loops refine the network's internal representations by reducing disagreement between what a layer predicts and what the adjacent layer represents.

Reusing these connections over time creates a longer sequence of nonlinear transformations. When the recurrent computation is unfolded, a network with few physical layers can act like an increasingly deep computation. The approach therefore makes repeated processing an explicit part of recognition, allowing representations to develop over successive rounds rather than being fixed after a single forward pass.

The paper evaluates image classification on SVHN, CIFAR, and ImageNet. Despite using notably fewer layers and parameters, the network achieves competitive performance against classical and state-of-the-art models. Further analysis finds that its representations converge over time and that recognition accuracy improves during recurrent processing. Top-down prediction errors also reveal visual saliency, connecting the same error signals used for refinement with a form of bottom-up attention.
neurips-2018-deep-predictive-coding-netw.tldr: A predictive coding network repeatedly exchanges predictions and errors between layers to improve object recognition with relatively few layers and parameters.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a multilayer neuronal network could learn toward a desired output using mechanisms compatible with features of cortical circuits. The proposed model gives neurons simplified dendritic compartments and uses different cell types. This organization allows a pyramidal neuron to represent both ordinary activity and an error signal.

Learning is driven continuously by local dendritic prediction errors, without requiring separate phases. These errors arise at apical dendrites when predictions supplied by lateral interneurons disagree with actual top-down feedback. Synaptic changes use those local mismatches while collectively adapting the network toward a global output target. The mechanism offers a concrete connection between locally available signals and learning across multiple layers.

The authors demonstrate learning on regression and classification tasks and analytically show that the model approximates backpropagation. They also report consistency with observations of learning between brain areas and with cortical microcircuit architecture. These results support a proposed account of how neural circuits may assign responsibility for an output error to individual synapses; they do not establish that the brain necessarily uses this mechanism.
neurips-2018-dendritic-cortical-microcir.tldr: A neuronal model uses continuous local dendritic errors to learn across layers and analytically approximate backpropagation.

paragraphs: Strongly Rayleigh distributions assign probabilities to subsets of a larger collection. Their strong negative dependence properties favor subsets containing diverse elements. The paper introduces an exponentiated version of this family, providing a way to adjust the strength of that behavior through one parameter rather than using a fixed degree of preference.

The exponent can be understood as an inverse temperature: it sharpens or smooths the distribution's negative dependence behavior. To make the resulting models usable, the authors develop efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo procedures for approximate sampling. They also derive explicit mixing-time bounds for exponentiated determinantal point processes and exponentiated dual volume sampling, describing how quickly those sampling procedures approach their target distributions.

The paper applies the models to several machine learning tasks and reports promising empirical results. The contribution combines a controllable family of distributions over subsets with algorithms for drawing approximate samples from them. Its theoretical sampling guarantees are given for two concrete instances, while the experiments illustrate the potential value of adjusting diversity-related behavior in applications.
neurips-2018-exponentiated-strongly-rayl.tldr: Exponentiated strongly Rayleigh distributions add a tunable diversity-related parameter and come with approximate sampling algorithms.

paragraphs: Standard variational autoencoders commonly assume that latent representations of different samples are independent and identically distributed. That assumption can be too restrictive when observations are related, as in an image time series. This paper introduces a Gaussian process prior variational autoencoder to represent correlations between samples within the latent model.

The approach combines the ability of a VAE to model complex observations with the covariance structure supplied by a Gaussian process. Accounting for relationships between observations can make the model better suited to the data and can help downstream tasks. To make inference efficient, the authors exploit structure in the covariance matrix and introduce a stochastic backpropagation strategy that computes gradients in a distributed, low-memory manner.

The method outperforms conditional VAEs and an adapted standard VAE in two image-data applications. These findings support the usefulness of modeling dependence between samples in those settings. The contribution includes both the richer prior and a computational strategy for training it, addressing the practical work needed to incorporate correlations into a VAE.
neurips-2018-gaussian-process-prior-vari.tldr: A Gaussian process prior lets a VAE model correlations between observations, with efficient training and improved results in two image applications.

paragraphs: Gen-Oja addresses principal generalized eigenvector computation and canonical correlation analysis in a stochastic setting. The paper proposes a simple, efficient algorithm for these problems, with streaming computation as its focus. Its central contribution is not only an update procedure but also a theoretical account of how that procedure converges.

The authors prove global convergence and show that the algorithm achieves an optimal convergence rate. Their analysis draws on fast-mixing Markov chains and stochastic approximation with two time scales. Bringing these ideas together provides a way to reason about the evolving stochastic process behind the computation and to establish how quickly the algorithm approaches its target.

In developing the proof, the paper also produces tools for studying stochastic processes with Markovian noise. Such noise has dependence across successive steps, making its behavior relevant to the analysis rather than something that can simply be treated as independent variation. The authors suggest that these tools may be useful beyond the two problems studied, giving the work a possible methodological contribution alongside its algorithmic guarantees.
neurips-2018-gen-oja-simple-efficient-al.tldr: Gen-Oja provides a simple stochastic algorithm for generalized eigenvectors and canonical correlation analysis with global convergence at an optimal rate.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a model trained on one source distribution can perform better on domains it has not seen. It frames learning around difficult alternative data distributions that remain near the source in feature space. That neighborhood defines the scope of the worst-case formulation and guides the construction of additional training examples.

The proposed procedure repeatedly creates examples from a fictitious target domain that is difficult for the current model, then appends them to the training data. Because the challenging examples change with the model, this is an adaptive form of adversarial data augmentation. The procedure needs training data from only a single source distribution.

For softmax losses, the authors show that the method can also be understood as data-dependent regularization. Its behavior differs from regularizers such as ridge and lasso that push parameters toward zero. Experiments on digit recognition and semantic segmentation show improved performance across multiple target domains that were unknown beforehand. The findings support using model-dependent training challenges to improve transfer in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2018-generalizing-to-unseen-doma.tldr: Iteratively adding adversarial examples from difficult nearby distributions improves generalization to unseen domains in the tested tasks.

paragraphs: Low-bitwidth neural networks reduce the precision used to represent parameters, making compact and fast implementations possible. Common approaches assign the same bitwidth across a layer or an entire model. This paper instead allows individual parameters to use different bitwidths, motivated by hardware that can efficiently support arithmetic instructions with customized precision.

The authors show that selecting bitwidths at the level of individual parameters during training is feasible and useful. Their examples include AlexNet and MobileNet models that mix 1-, 2-, and 3-bit parameters. With an appropriate mix averaging 1.4 bits per parameter, these networks can match the accuracy of corresponding homogeneous 2-bit versions.

The significance is that precision need not be allocated uniformly to preserve the demonstrated accuracy. Hardware analyses further indicate that the heterogeneous designs yield FPGA and ASIC implementations with better circuit-area and energy efficiency than their homogeneous counterparts. The paper therefore connects a training-time choice about parameter representation to both predictive performance and the efficiency of specialized hardware implementations.
neurips-2018-heterogeneous-bitwidth-bina.tldr: Choosing bitwidths per parameter can match homogeneous 2-bit network accuracy at an average of 1.4 bits while improving hardware efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper studies when a network contains insufficient information to recover the labels of its nodes. It considers several ways networks can be generated, including stochastic block, exponential random graph, latent space, directed preferential attachment, and directed small-world models. The focus is on fundamental non-recoverability conditions, rather than the performance of a particular detection algorithm.

The relevant obstacles depend on the network model. For the stochastic block model, the condition involves the probabilities of edges within and between communities. For the latent space model, it depends on the space's dimension and on how far apart and how spread out the communities are. These results link recovery limits to the mechanisms that make communities distinguishable in each model.

For directed preferential attachment and directed small-world models, the non-recoverability condition depends on the ratio of homophily to neighborhood size. The analysis also covers dynamic versions of the stochastic block and latent space models. Together, these results identify model-dependent barriers that an algorithm cannot overcome merely by using a different computational strategy when the stated non-recoverability conditions hold.
neurips-2018-information-theoretic-limit.tldr: The paper derives model-dependent conditions under which network node labels cannot be recovered from the available information.

paragraphs: The paper investigates which part of a variational autoencoder's training objective is connected to learning disentangled representations. It decomposes the evidence lower bound and identifies a term measuring total correlation among latent variables. This makes dependence between latent variables an explicit component of the objective that can be examined separately.

That decomposition motivates beta-TCVAE, a refinement of beta-VAE designed for learning disentangled representations. The proposed algorithm can replace beta-VAE without adding training hyperparameters. The paper also introduces the mutual information gap, or MIG, as a principled measure of disentanglement that does not require a classifier. The contributions therefore address both how such representations are learned and how they are evaluated.

Quantitative and qualitative experiments cover both restricted and non-restricted settings. Within the proposed training framework, the authors find a strong relationship between total correlation and disentanglement. This connects an identifiable mathematical term to observed representation behavior, helping isolate a source of disentanglement in the studied models. The stated relationship is tied to that framework rather than presented as a universal equivalence.
neurips-2018-isolating-sources-of-disent.tldr: Beta-TCVAE isolates total correlation in the VAE objective and links it to disentanglement, while MIG provides a classifier-free evaluation measure.

paragraphs: In games with asymmetric information, an agent's behavior can reveal or conceal what it is trying to accomplish. This paper uses that idea to learn cooperative or competitive strategies without a model of the other agent or interaction with it during learning. The agent is encouraged to make its intentions more or less informative through an information-theoretic regularizer.

The authors consider two quantities: the mutual information between goal and action given the current state, and the mutual information between goal and state. These capture different ways behavior can carry information about an agent's objective. The paper develops stochastic methods for optimizing both regularizers that can be integrated into policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

In two simple asymmetric-information games, policies trained to cooperate lead to greater reward for a second agent, while policies trained to compete lead to lower reward for that agent. The experiments show that controlling how much goal information an agent exposes can affect another agent's success, even when the learning procedure does not directly model or interact with that other agent.
neurips-2018-learning-to-share-and-hide-.tldr: Information regularization teaches agents to reveal or hide their goals, helping or hindering another agent in two asymmetric-information games.

paragraphs: Objects such as faces and flowers can have symmetric structure even when their photographs do not look symmetric. Articulation and perspective can obscure that structure in the image. This paper proposes learning object symmetries from images without manual supervision, addressing the difficulty of relying on an underlying three-dimensional shape that may not be reliably recoverable.

The key move is to seek symmetry in the space of object deformations. The authors extend an object frame representation so that object symmetries become straightforward symmetry groups in a normalized space. This lets the method learn from an unstructured collection of object images, using the representation to expose regularity that need not be visually obvious in any individual photograph.

The formulation also explains ambiguities in recovering the pose of a symmetric object from its shape or images. Symmetry can leave multiple pose interpretations compatible with the available appearance. The paper provides a way to discount these ambiguities during learning, connecting its representation of symmetry with the practical problem of learning pose-related structure from ambiguous observations.
neurips-2018-modelling-and-unsupervised-.tldr: The method learns object symmetries from unlabeled images by representing them through deformations in a normalized object space.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval aims to reconstruct a signal from quadratic observations. This paper assumes the signal lies in the output range of a generative neural network with a k-dimensional input. That structural prior offers another route beyond sparsity-based methods, for which the abstract describes a gap between known efficient recovery guarantees and the theoretical measurement optimum.

Under a model of a fully connected multilayer network with random weights, the proposed empirical risk has favorable global geometry with O(k) measurements. Specifically, a descent direction exists outside small neighborhoods of the true latent code and a negative multiple of it. This is a conditional geometric result supporting gradient-based optimization under the stated network model.

The formulation can exploit a generative prior at an information-theoretically optimal sample complexity. Generative priors can also represent natural signals more tightly than generic sparsity priors. Experiments report better phase-retrieval performance than sparse and general methods. The theoretical and empirical contributions together support the approach, while the random-weight model remains an explicit condition of the geometry analysis.
neurips-2018-phase-retrieval-under-a-gen.tldr: A generative prior yields favorable phase-retrieval geometry with O(k) measurements under a random-network model and performs well in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper considers a team of reinforcement learning agents operating concurrently in a common environment. It develops an approach to coordinated exploration intended to work at practical scales. The objective is to make the team's exploration effective when several agents are learning at once, including settings that require a richer representation than a table.

The approach combines seed sampling with a randomized value-function learning algorithm. These are the two foundations of the proposed exploration method. The study evaluates the combination in both simple tabular settings and a higher-dimensional problem using a neural network to represent the value function, directly examining its use across different levels of representation complexity.

In the tabular experiments, the method is competitive with earlier approaches considered by the authors. In the higher-dimensional setting, it learns quickly using far fewer agents than alternative exploration schemes. That finding supports the practical aim of effective exploration without needing a large concurrent team in the tested problem. The abstract presents this scaling benefit as an experimental result.
neurips-2018-scalable-coordinated-explor.tldr: Combining seed sampling with randomized value learning enables effective coordinated exploration, using fewer agents in a tested higher-dimensional problem.

paragraphs: This paper presents a lightweight way to embed probabilistic programming in a deep learning ecosystem. It organizes the interface around a single abstraction, the random variable, and implements the approach in TensorFlow. The aim is to make probabilistic models and inference work with the distributed computation and accelerators available in that environment.

The implementation supports several distinct applications: a model-parallel variational autoencoder, a data-parallel Image Transformer, and a multi-GPU No-U-Turn Sampler. These examples span neural generative modeling and sampling-based inference. They demonstrate that the same low-level approach can support different computational arrangements rather than being tied to one model or one way of dividing work.

For a VAE on 64×64 ImageNet and an Image Transformer on 256×256 CelebA-HQ, the authors report optimal linear speedup from 1 to 256 TPUv2 chips. For NUTS on GPUs, they report speedups of 100 times over Stan and 37 times over PyMC3. These results show substantial acceleration for the demonstrated applications while retaining a simple probabilistic programming abstraction.
neurips-2018-simple-distributed-and-acce.tldr: A random-variable-based TensorFlow implementation supports distributed probabilistic programming with strong accelerator speedups in demonstrated applications.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a primal-dual homotopy smoothing algorithm for convex optimization with linear constraints. Neither the primal nor the dual function needs to be smooth or strongly convex. Its goal is to improve the iteration complexity for this nonsmooth problem class by using additional local structure in the dual function.

The improvement depends on a local error bound condition with parameter β between zero and one. Under that condition, the algorithm achieves primal convergence time O(ε^(-2/(2+β)) log₂(ε⁻¹)), improving on the stated O(ε⁻¹) benchmark. The result therefore identifies a sufficient structural condition for faster convergence without imposing smoothness or strong convexity on the functions.

As a concrete application, the authors analyze the distributed geometric median problem. Its dual is nonsmooth but satisfies the required condition with β = 1/2, yielding a bound of O(ε^(-4/5) log₂(ε⁻¹)). This improves the convergence-time bound of existing distributed optimization algorithms described in the abstract. Simulations also demonstrate the proposed method's performance, complementing the conditional complexity result with computational evidence.
neurips-2018-solving-non-smooth-constrai.tldr: A primal-dual smoothing method improves nonsmooth constrained optimization complexity when the dual satisfies a local error bound.

paragraphs: Blind deconvolution tries to recover two unknown signals from their convolution, a problem that is ill-posed in general. This paper studies a structured version in which one signal is short and the other has sparse, randomly located support. The short signal is assumed to have unit Euclidean norm, allowing recovery to be formulated as nonconvex optimization over a sphere.

The first result describes the structure of local optima within a particular region of that sphere. Every local optimum there is close to a shifted and truncated version of the true short signal. This gives useful meaning to those optima, while keeping the geometric claim restricted to the region analyzed.

The second result gives a recovery guarantee for a generic short signal of length k when activation sparsity satisfies θ ≲ k^(-2/3) and the measurement count is at least polynomial in k. Under these conditions, a simple initialization followed by descent that escapes strict saddle points recovers a near shifted truncation of the true kernel. The guarantee concerns this structured approximation, rather than unrestricted exact recovery.
neurips-2018-structured-local-minima-in-.tldr: Under stated sparsity and measurement conditions, nonconvex blind deconvolution recovers an approximation to a shifted truncation of the true short signal.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether speech and text representations can be aligned without paired audio-text training examples. It takes inspiration from unsupervised alignment between text embedding spaces in different languages and extends the goal across modalities. The framework first learns speech and text embedding spaces from their respective corpora.

It then attempts to align those spaces using adversarial training, followed by a refinement procedure. The important distinction is that the alignment is learned without parallel supervision connecting the two modalities. This makes the approach relevant when speech and text resources exist separately but matched recordings and transcriptions are scarce.

The authors demonstrate uses in spoken word classification and translation. On those two tasks, the unsupervised alignment achieves performance comparable to a supervised counterpart. The paper also identifies potential value for speech recognition and speech-to-text translation in low- or zero-resource languages. The reported experiments support the alignment approach on the evaluated tasks, while the broader speech-system applications describe why such an approach could be useful.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-cross-modal-al.tldr: Adversarial alignment and refinement connect independently learned speech and text embeddings without paired supervision, with competitive results on two word-level tasks.

paragraphs: The paper learns visual landmarks, such as facial feature locations, without manually labeled examples. It turns landmark learning into an image-generation task: combine the appearance of an object from one image with its geometry from another. The paired examples differ through a viewpoint change, object deformation, or both.

A tight bottleneck in the geometry-extraction process selects and compresses geometry-related information. This encourages the model to separate object layout from appearance while learning features useful for generating the requested image. Because both appearance and geometry condition the output, the task is substantially less ambiguous than standard image generation. The authors find that a simple perceptual loss is sufficient.

The approach learns landmarks from synthetic image deformations or videos and outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised landmark detectors in the reported evaluation. It also applies without modification to datasets containing faces, people, three-dimensional objects, and digits. The findings show how a carefully structured generation task can provide the learning signal for landmark detection across several kinds of visual data without manual supervision.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-learning-of-ob.tldr: Conditioning image generation on separate appearance and compressed geometry signals teaches landmark detection without manual labels.

paragraphs: Positive alpha-divergences are useful in variational inference because they encourage an approximation to cover probability mass. However, estimating and optimizing them requires importance sampling, whose weights can have heavy tails. The resulting variance can be extremely large or even infinite, creating a difficulty in using the desired divergence reliably.

The paper introduces tail-adaptive f-divergences to address this problem. Instead of keeping the defining convex function fixed, the method adapts it to the tail behavior of the importance weights. The authors provide theoretical guarantees of finite moments while retaining mass-covering properties. This connects the choice of divergence directly to the statistical behavior of the weights used during optimization.

The methods are tested on Bayesian neural networks and deep reinforcement learning, where they are used to improve a soft actor-critic algorithm. The reported results show significant advantages over methods based on classical KL and alpha-divergences. Together, the theory and experiments support adapting the divergence to control problematic weight tails while preserving the intended coverage behavior.
neurips-2018-variational-inference-with-.tldr: Tail-adaptive divergences retain mass-covering behavior while guaranteeing finite moments through adaptation to importance-weight tails.

paragraphs: Random forests average predictions from many randomized trees. This paper examines how tree construction and parameter choices affect generalization as the amount of training data grows without bound. The focus is consistency: whether a forest's prediction behavior approaches the appropriate large-sample target, rather than merely whether it performs well on a particular finite dataset.

The analysis identifies subsampling during tree construction as important. Forests can be inconsistent when they use no subsampling, but they can also be inconsistent when subsampling is too severe. Even heavily randomized trees can produce inconsistent forests without subsampling. Thus, adding randomness to the trees does not by itself prevent the failure modes established by the analysis.

The results imply that some commonly used random-forest configurations can be inconsistent. They also show that tree constructions effective for nearest-neighbor search can be poor choices for random-forest prediction. These findings make the construction details consequential: a tree's usefulness for another task, or its high degree of randomization, does not establish the long-run predictive properties of the resulting forest.
neurips-2018-when-do-random-forests-fail.tldr: Random forests can be inconsistent with either absent or overly severe subsampling, even when their trees are highly randomized.

paragraphs: This paper argues that unfair predictions should be examined in the context of the data used to train and evaluate a model. Inadequate sample sizes and missing predictive variables can contribute to discrimination. When those are the causes, the authors advocate addressing them through data collection rather than relying on constraints imposed on the model.

The proposed analysis decomposes cost-based discrimination metrics into bias, variance, and noise. The authors then suggest actions for estimating and reducing each component. This makes the observed discrimination something to investigate by source, helping connect a measured disparity with a possible intervention instead of treating every disparity as the same modeling problem.

Case studies involving income, mortality, and review-rating prediction support the value of the analysis. The authors find that collecting data can often reduce discrimination without sacrificing accuracy. That qualified finding matters in sensitive settings where additional prediction errors can have serious consequences. The contribution is a way to diagnose data-related causes of unfairness and identify opportunities to improve fairness and accuracy together.
neurips-2018-why-is-my-classifier-discri.tldr: Decomposing discrimination into bias, variance, and noise can reveal data-collection opportunities that reduce unfairness without sacrificing accuracy.
